title: Plane Fuel Costs More Than Ever, and Holiday Flights Cost More Too
summary:
Are you flying somewhere for the holidays? Get ready: tickets may cost a lot more this year.

The main reason is jet fuel, the special fuel airplanes burn. It is one of the biggest costs for airlines. On Thursday, the average price of jet fuel in the United States reached $4.90 a gallon, according to the tracking firm Argus. That is the highest one-day average Argus has ever recorded, and more than double the price a year ago.

Airlines are passing part of the cost to passengers. Airfares are at a 10-year high, said Hayley Berg, the lead economist at Hopper, a travel tech company. Thanksgiving tickets cost about 30% more than last year, and Christmas tickets are up more than 20%.

Still, people keep booking. Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian said travelers still see tickets as fairly affordable. Chris Sununu, head of the trade group Airlines for America, said airlines are paying most of the extra fuel cost themselves, but some must be passed on to customers.

Families are coping in different ways. Many booked trips earlier than usual to lock in lower prices. Rachel Stern of Frederick, Maryland, said tickets for her and her kids cost too much, so she will drive to Chicago instead.
why_it_matters: If your family flies to visit relatives for the holidays, higher ticket prices could change how — or whether — you make the trip.

background_read: Airplanes burn a special fuel called jet fuel, and it is one of the biggest costs for airlines.
When jet fuel gets more expensive, airlines often pass part of that extra cost on to the people buying tickets.
That is why flights can cost more at busy travel times like Thanksgiving and Christmas, when many families fly to visit each other.
